# End-of-Chapter Exercise Solutions {#sec-exercise-solutions}



This appendix collects worked solutions for the **end-of-chapter exercises** that follow the *Quick checks* section in each chapter.

Each entry shows the question — *click to expand* — followed by the solution. References point back to the section of the chapter the exercise is testing.

If you spot an error or have a suggested improvement, please [file an issue](https://github.com/moderndive/ModernDive_book/issues) or open a pull request against the `v2-quarto-html` branch.

***

## Chapter 4 Solutions


Solutions for the end-of-chapter exercises in @sec-tidy. The dataset is `bob_ross` from the [`fivethirtyeight`](https://fivethirtyeight-r.netlify.app/reference/bob_ross.html) package: 403 episodes × 71 columns (4 identifiers + 67 binary indicator columns).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
library(fivethirtyeight)
```
:::


### Setup and first look

***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.2 — show question"}
**EX4.2 (★)** The first four columns of `bob_ross` (`episode`, `season`, `episode_num`, `title`) are *identification* variables, not *measurement* variables. Explain in one sentence why. *(@sec-tidy-definition)*
:::

**Solution.** They serve to **uniquely identify** which episode each row refers to (e.g., `S01E01` titled "A Walk in the Woods"); they describe *which* observation we're looking at, not *what* was painted in it.

***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.3 — show question"}
**EX4.3 (★)** Without running any code, predict: what are the only two possible values that any of the 67 indicator columns (e.g., `mountain`, `tree`) can take? Then verify by running `summary(bob_ross$tree)`. *(@sec-tidy-definition)*
:::

**Solution.** The columns are **0/1 indicators** — `1` means the element appears in that episode, `0` means it does not.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(bob_ross$tree)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.0000  1.0000  1.0000  0.8958  1.0000  1.0000 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
range(bob_ross$tree)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0 1
```


:::
:::


***

**EX4.4 (★)** Count how many episodes feature a `cabin`. Hint: an indicator column of 0/1 sums to the number of 1s. *(@sec-tidy-data-ex)*
:::

**Solution.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(bob_ross$cabin)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 69
```

***

### Recognizing tidy structure

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.5 — show question"}
**EX4.5 (★)** Is `bob_ross` in tidy format? Justify by referring to the three rules from @sec-tidy-definition. *(@sec-tidy-definition)*
:::

**Solution.** **No.** Two of Wickham's three rules are violated:

1. *Each variable is a column.* ✗ — there are really only two variables encoded across the 67 indicator columns: the **element name** (currently a column name) and **whether it appeared** (currently a cell value).
2. *Each observation is a row.* ✗ — the natural observation is "this element in this episode," but right now one row holds 67 such observations.
3. *Each observational unit has its own table.* ✓.

The fix is `pivot_longer()` (see EX4.9).

***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.6 — show question"}
**EX4.6 (★)** Two variables are encoded in the *names* of the 67 indicator columns. What are they? *(@sec-tidy-definition)*
:::

**Solution.** The column **names** encode the variable **`element`** (e.g., `mountain`, `cabin`, `tree`), and the **cell values** encode the variable **`present`** (0 or 1). Both should be their own columns in tidy form.

***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.7 — show question"}
**EX4.7 (★★)** The `episode` column contains values like `"S01E01"`, `"S01E02"`. How many distinct pieces of information are packed into this single column? Suggest tidier columns to replace it. *(@sec-tidy-definition)*
:::

**Solution.** Two: the **season number** and the **episode-within-season number**. They are already separated into the `season` and `episode_num` columns, so `episode` is technically redundant — though useful as a human-readable label. A `tidyr::separate()` call would split `"S01E01"` into the two pieces if the columns weren't already present:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tibble(episode = c("S01E01", "S02E13")) |>
  separate_wider_position(episode, widths = c(s = 1, season = 2, e = 1, ep = 2))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  s     season e     ep   
  <chr> <chr>  <chr> <chr>
1 S     01     E     01   
2 S     02     E     13   
```


:::
:::


***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.8 — show question"}
**EX4.8 (★)** What is the *observational unit* of `bob_ross`? Phrase your answer as "one row of `bob_ross` represents one ____." *(@sec-tidy-definition)*
:::

**Solution.** One row of `bob_ross` represents one **episode** of *The Joy of Painting*.

***

### Pivoting longer

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.9 — show question"}
**EX4.9 (★★)** Use `pivot_longer()` to reshape `bob_ross` so that all 67 indicator columns become two columns: one called `element` (the old name) and one called `present` (the 0/1 value). Save the result to `bob_long`. *(@sec-tidyverse-package)*
:::

**Solution.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bob_long <- bob_ross |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = -c(episode, season, episode_num, title),
    names_to  = "element",
    values_to = "present"
  )

bob_long
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 27,001 × 6
   episode season episode_num title               element         present
   <chr>    <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>               <chr>             <int>
 1 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS apple_frame           0
 2 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS aurora_borealis       0
 3 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS barn                  0
 4 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS beach                 0
 5 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS boat                  0
 6 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS bridge                0
 7 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS building              0
 8 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS bushes                1
 9 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS cabin                 0
10 S01E01       1           1 A WALK IN THE WOODS cactus                0
# ℹ 26,991 more rows
```


:::
:::


***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.10 — show question"}
**EX4.10 (★★)** `bob_ross` has 403 rows and 67 indicator columns. **Predict** the number of rows in `bob_long` *before* you check. Then verify with `nrow()`. *(@sec-tidyverse-package)*
:::

**Solution.** Predicted: $403 \times 67 = 27{,}001$ rows. Verified:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(bob_long)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 27001
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
403 * 67
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 27001
```


:::
:::


***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.11 — show question"}
**EX4.11 (★★)** After pivoting, each row of `bob_long` represents one ___ in one ___. Fill in the blanks. *(@sec-tidy-definition)*
:::

**Solution.** Each row represents **one element in one episode** — e.g., "was `mountain` present in `S01E03`?".

***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.12 — show question"}
**EX4.12 (★★)** Filter `bob_long` to rows where `present == 1` and call the result `bob_present`. How many rows does it have, and what does that count tell you about the show as a whole? *(@sec-tidy-data-ex)*
:::

**Solution.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bob_present <- bob_long |> filter(present == 1)
nrow(bob_present)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3221
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(bob_present) / 403   # average elements per episode
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 7.992556
```


:::
:::


The total — the count of element-episode pairs where `present == 1` — divided by 403 episodes gives the **mean number of elements per painting** (≈10).

***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.13 — show question"}
**EX4.13 (★★)** Why does using `cols = -c(episode, season, episode_num, title)` work *better* than listing all 67 element columns by name in `pivot_longer()`? *(@sec-tidyverse-package)*
:::

**Solution.** *Negative selection* (`-c(...)`) means "everything except these four." It's **shorter**, **less error-prone** (no risk of typos in 67 column names), and **future-proof**: if FiveThirtyEight ever adds a new element column, the code keeps working without changes.

***

### Summarizing the long-form data

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.14 — show question"}
**EX4.14 (★★)** Using `bob_long` (or `bob_present`), find the **top 10 most-painted elements** across all episodes. *(@sec-tidy-data-ex)*
:::

**Solution.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bob_long |>
  group_by(element) |>
  summarize(n_episodes = sum(present)) |>
  arrange(desc(n_episodes)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

   element   n_episodes
   <chr>          <int>
 1 tree             361
 2 trees            337
 3 deciduous        227
 4 conifer          212
 5 clouds           179
 6 mountain         160
 7 lake             143
 8 grass            142
 9 river            126
10 bushes           120
```


:::
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.16 — show question"}
**EX4.16 (★★)** Compute the *average number of elements per painting* across the full series. Is this larger or smaller than you would have guessed? *(@sec-tidy-data-ex)*

***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.17 — show question"}
**EX4.17 (★★)** Did Bob Ross ever paint a `barn`? In how many episodes? In what fraction of his run does a barn appear? *(@sec-tidy-data-ex)*
:::

**Solution.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bob_long |>
  filter(element == "barn") |>
  summarize(
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.18 — show question"}
**EX4.18 (★★)** Which episode features the *largest* number of distinct elements? Print its `episode`, `title`, and total element count. *(@sec-tidy-data-ex)*
:::

**Solution.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bob_long |>
  group_by(episode, title) |>
  summarize(n_elements = sum(present), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(n_elements, n = 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

  episode title         n_elements
  <chr>   <chr>              <int>
1 S10E09  MOUNTAIN OVAL         15
```

***

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.19 — show question"}
**EX4.19 (★★★)** For each season, find the **single most-painted element**. Are there elements that dominate one season but not another? *(@sec-tidy-data-ex)*
:::

**Solution.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bob_long |>
  group_by(season, element) |>
  summarize(n_episodes = sum(present), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  slice_max(n_episodes, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(season)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

10     10 tree            11
# ℹ 21 more rows
```

`tree` and `tree_s` (plural) appear at the top across nearly every season — Bob really did love trees.

### Visualizing the long-form data

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.20 — show question"}
**EX4.20 (★★)** Build a horizontal bar chart of the top 15 elements by total appearance count across the full series. *(@sec-tidy-data-ex)*
:::

**Solution.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
top15 <- bob_long |>
  group_by(element) |>
  summarize(n = sum(present)) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 15)

ggplot(top15, aes(x = n, y = reorder(element, n))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Episodes featuring element", y = NULL,
       title = "Top 15 elements across The Joy of Painting")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.26 — show question"}
**EX4.26 (★)** What is the difference between `library(tidyverse)` and `library(tidyr)`? Which one would suffice for the pivots in this set of exercises, and which is more convenient? *(@sec-tidyverse-package)*
:::

**Solution.** `library(tidyr)` loads only the `tidyr` package — which is enough for `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`. `library(tidyverse)` is the **umbrella** package that loads `tidyr`, `dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `readr`, and several others in a single call. The umbrella is more convenient when you want all the tidyverse tools at once, as we did throughout this exercise set.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="EX4.29 — show question"}
**EX4.29 (★★★)** Name **two** questions about Bob Ross's painting style that this dataset *cannot* answer. For each, explain what additional data you would need. *(@sec-tidy-data-ex)*
:::

**Solution.** *Answers will vary.* Examples:

1. *"Which colors did Bob use most often?"* — the dataset records **what objects** appeared, not paint pigments or palette choices. You'd need each episode's full color list.
2. *"How long did each painting take to complete?"* — the dataset has no runtime or stroke-count information. You'd need video timing data or the show's production records.
